E6.question: What evidence-based guidance exists for communicating non-diagnostic screening results, stating limitations, and suggesting referral/support pathways for college students without providing treatment prescriptions?
E6.answer: Guidance emphasizes that screening is a proactive, systematic process designed to identify both strengths and needs across the entire student population, rather than solely targeting those already displaying concerns. When communicating results, it is important to acknowledge that a complaint-based approach may under-detect symptoms because students may mask mental health issues or report somatic complaints to avoid stigma. For college students who screen positive, the recommended pathway involves further evaluation using more detailed instruments, such as progressing from the PHQ-2 to the PHQ-9. Ultimately, screening results should guide the student toward appropriate support, which may include referral to counseling services, while also promoting comprehensive, multi-tiered support strategies.

contexts: 3 School mental health screening is defined as the use of a systematic tool or process to identify the strengths and needs of students. Screening is conducted for all students, not just students identified as being at risk for or already displaying mental health concerns. This might involve screening an entire population, such as a school’s student body, or a smaller subset of a population, such as a specific grade level. Most commonly, mental health screening is used to identify individual students who are experiencing or are at risk of experiencing social, emotional, and/or behavioral difficulties. The use of screening as an early identification strategy detects the onset of challenges early so that they can be addressed before they escalate. Screening measures can also ask students about: • indicators of well-being and positive mental health • life satisfaction • school belonging • social determinants of mental health • adverse early life experiences What is School Mental Health Screening? DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 6 injury, and possibly suicide (Pedrelli el al., 2015). Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified.
